claim: Primary hippocampal neuron cultures were sparsely transfected with the glutamate sensor iGluSnFR under control of a neuronal promoter (synapsin-1).
source: Primary hippocampal neuron cultures were sparsely transfected with the glutamate sensor iGluSnFR under control of a neuronal promoter (synapsin-1).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental procedure used in the study.

claim: iGluSnFR expression did not significantly change the density of excitatory synapses.
source: We found that iGluSnFR expression did not significantly change the density of excitatory synapses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B), indicating that expression of iGluSnFR at the plasma membrane does not disrupt synaptic organization.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing synapse density in iGluSnFR transfected neurons with control groups, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Expression of iGluSnFR at the plasma membrane does not disrupt synaptic organization.
source: We found that iGluSnFR expression did not significantly change the density of excitatory synapses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B), indicating that expression of iGluSnFR at the plasma membrane does not disrupt synaptic organization.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that synapse density was not affected by iGluSnFR expression.

claim: iGluSnFR has a greater density at synaptic regions.
source: After applying clustering analysis using density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (DBSCAN) (Sawant, 2014), we observed that iGluSnFR has a greater density at synaptic regions (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by super resolution microscopy data analyzed using DBSCAN clustering analysis, as shown in Figure 1B, C.

claim: Pair correlation analysis of iGluSnFR clusters that colocalized with the postsynaptic marker PSD95 revealed an increased clustering of iGluSnFR near the center of the synapse, compared to a theoretical random distribution.
source: Pair correlation analysis of iGluSnFR clusters that colocalized with the postsynaptic marker PSD95 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B), revealed an increased clustering of iGluSnFR near the center of the synapse, compared to a theoretical random distribution (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by pair correlation analysis data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: There exists a general trapping mechanism at dendritic spines that confines iGluSnFR.
source: This suggests the existence of a general trapping mechanism at dendritic spines that confines iGluSnFR.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of increased clustering of iGluSnFR near the center of synapses.

claim: Pr has been widely reported to be low and highly variable at individual hippocampal synapses, in culture as well as in intact tissue, ranging from 0.1 to 0.2 to 0.6.
source: Pr has been widely reported to be low and highly variable at individual hippocampal synapses, in culture as well as in intact tissue, ranging from 0.1 to 0.2 to 0.6 (Branco et al., 2008; Chanaday and Kavalali, 2018; Farsi et al., 2021; Jensen et al., 2021; Leitz and Kavalali, 2011; Murthy et al., 1997; Tagliatti et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: iGluSnFR reported a low average release probability that was also highly variable among synapses.
source: Accordingly, iGluSnFR reported a low average release probability that was also highly variable among synapses (Figure 2E–G), indicating that each ROI contained a single synapse.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E–G.

claim: Each ROI contained a single synapse.
source: Accordingly, iGluSnFR reported a low average release probability that was also highly variable among synapses (Figure 2E–G), indicating that each ROI contained a single synapse.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that release probability was low and variable, consistent with single synapse measurements.

claim: Pr is positively regulated by extracellular Ca2+ levels.
source: Pr is positively regulated by extracellular Ca2+ levels (Chanaday and Kavalali, 2018; Leitz and Kavalali, 2011; Murthy et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In iGluSnFR transfected neurons, perfusion of solutions with increasing Ca2+ concentrations leads to a corresponding increase of Pr.
source: In iGluSnFR transfected neurons, perfusion of solutions with increasing Ca2+ concentrations leads to a corresponding increase of Pr (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E, F.

claim: Glutamate release is completely abrogated in the absence of extracellular calcium.
source: Glutamate release is completely abrogated in the absence of extracellular calcium (Figure 2F), while Pr values are shifted toward high probabilities of 0.86 ± 0.23 in 8 mM Ca2+, compared to 2 mM at 0.49 ± 0.32 (Figure 2G, H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Pr values are shifted toward high probabilities of 0.86 ± 0.23 in 8 mM Ca2+, compared to 2 mM at 0.49 ± 0.32.
source: Glutamate release is completely abrogated in the absence of extracellular calcium (Figure 2F), while Pr values are shifted toward high probabilities of 0.86 ± 0.23 in 8 mM Ca2+, compared to 2 mM at 0.49 ± 0.32 (Figure 2G, H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G, H.

claim: The peak amplitudes increased at higher extracellular Ca2+ concentrations.
source: We found that the peak amplitudes increased at higher extracellular Ca2+ concentrations (Figure 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The increase in peak amplitudes at higher Ca2+ concentrations could be due to multivesicular release as release probabilities increase at higher Ca2+ concentrations, or glutamate spill over from adjacent sites, or a combination of these factors.
source: Based on the literature, this could be due to multivesicular release as release probabilities increase at higher Ca2+ concentrations (Leitz and Kavalali, 2011; Rudolph et al., 2015), or glutamate spill over from adjacent sites (Armbruster et al., 2020), or a combination of these factors.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Individual spontaneous glutamate release events can be detected at synapses with a high signal-to-noise ratio, similar to that of evoked events.
source: We were able to detect individual spontaneous glutamate release events at synapses with a high signal-to-noise ratio, similar to that of evoked events (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, B.

claim: The average frequency of spontaneous events has been reported to be approximately 0.01–0.02 Hz per synapse.
source: The average frequency of spontaneous events has been reported to be approximately 0.01–0.02 Hz per synapse (Geppert et al., 1994; Leitz and Kavalali, 2014; Murthy and Stevens, 1999; Reese and Kavalali, 2016) and our detection of spontaneous events using iGluSnFR is comparable to this value (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Detection of spontaneous events using iGluSnFR is comparable to the reported value of approximately 0.01–0.02 Hz per synapse.
source: The average frequency of spontaneous events has been reported to be approximately 0.01–0.02 Hz per synapse (Geppert et al., 1994; Leitz and Kavalali, 2014; Murthy and Stevens, 1999; Reese and Kavalali, 2016) and our detection of spontaneous events using iGluSnFR is comparable to this value (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and comparison to cited literature values.

claim: At individual synapses, both evoked and spontaneous neurotransmission lead to release of one synaptic vesicle, thereby activating a similar numbers of probes and leading to similar event amplitudes.
source: Thus, at individual synapses, both evoked and spontaneous neurotransmission lead to release of one synaptic vesicle, thereby activating a similar numbers of probes and leading to similar event amplitudes (Leitz and Kavalali, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study and established knowledge about quantal release.

claim: Comparable peak amplitudes were measured for evoked and spontaneous events.
source: Based on this, we expect to find similar results using iGluSnFR, and indeed we measured comparable peak amplitudes for evoked and spontaneous events (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The comparable peak amplitudes for evoked and spontaneous events provide further support that the study is detecting the release of single synaptic vesicles at single synapses.
source: This provides further support that we are detecting the release of single synaptic vesicles at single synapses.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of comparable peak amplitudes.

claim: When release properties were analyzed at the level of individual synapses, spontaneous neurotransmission rate and evoked release probability did not correlate within synapses.
source: When release properties were analyzed at the level of individual synapses, spontaneous neurotransmission rate and evoked release probability did not correlate within synapses (Figure 3E), similar to prior studies (Leitz and Kavalali, 2014; Reese and Kavalali, 2016), thus reinforcing that evoked and spontaneous neurotransmission are partially segregated.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and citations to prior studies.

claim: Evoked and spontaneous neurotransmission are partially segregated.
source: When release properties were analyzed at the level of individual synapses, spontaneous neurotransmission rate and evoked release probability did not correlate within synapses (Figure 3E), similar to prior studies (Leitz and Kavalali, 2014; Reese and Kavalali, 2016), thus reinforcing that evoked and spontaneous neurotransmission are partially segregated.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of correlation between spontaneous rate and evoked release probability, supported by data and citations.

claim: The spontaneous event frequency in a bath solution containing CNQX and APV is not significantly different than in CNQX, APV, and the action potential blocker tetrodotoxin (TTX).
source: Importantly, we observed that the spontaneous event frequency in a bath solution containing CNQX and APV (which blocks AMPAR and NMDARs, respectively) is not significantly different than in CNQX, APV, and the action potential blocker tetrodotoxin (TTX (Figure 3F)), demonstrating that inhibition of ionotropic glutamate receptors is sufficient to suppress action potential-driven release.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Inhibition of ionotropic glutamate receptors is sufficient to suppress action potential-driven release.
source: Importantly, we observed that the spontaneous event frequency in a bath solution containing CNQX and APV (which blocks AMPAR and NMDARs, respectively) is not significantly different than in CNQX, APV, and the action potential blocker tetrodotoxin (TTX (Figure 3F)), demonstrating that inhibition of ionotropic glutamate receptors is sufficient to suppress action potential-driven release.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that spontaneous event frequency was not different with or without TTX when ionotropic glutamate receptors were blocked.

claim: CNQX and APV do not interact with iGluSnFR.
source: Furthermore, these drugs do not interact with iGluSnFR (Marvin et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: All studies on spontaneous neurotransmission using iGluSnFR were performed in the presence of only CNQX and APV.
source: Thus, all studies on spontaneous neurotransmission using iGluSnFR were performed in the presence of only CNQX and APV.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental conditions used in the study.

claim: In 0 mM Ca2+, spontaneous release propensity is lower but not completely diminished.
source: In 0 mM Ca2+, spontaneous release propensity is lower but not completely diminished, and iGluSnFR event amplitudes remained unchanged (Figure 3H, I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H, I.

claim: iGluSnFR event amplitudes remained unchanged in 0 mM Ca2+.
source: In 0 mM Ca2+, spontaneous release propensity is lower but not completely diminished, and iGluSnFR event amplitudes remained unchanged (Figure 3H, I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H, I.

claim: The observation that spontaneous release is lower but not completely diminished in 0 mM Ca2+ is consistent with previous studies demonstrating that spontaneous release is less sensitive to reductions in bath Ca2+ than evoked release.
source: This is consistent with previous studies demonstrating that spontaneous release is less sensitive to reductions in bath Ca2+ than evoked release (Kavalali, 2020; Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hypertonic sucrose has been shown to trigger the fusion of docked synaptic vesicles in an action potential and Ca2+-independent manner.
source: Hypertonic sucrose has been shown to trigger the fusion of docked synaptic vesicles in an action potential and Ca2+-independent manner (Rosenmund and Stevens, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: High hypertonicity (+300 to +500 mOsm) causes the whole readily releasable pool to rapidly fuse.
source: While high hypertonicity (+300 to +500 mOsm) causes the whole readily releasable pool to rapidly fuse, individual release events can be resolved at lower sucrose concentrations (+100 mOsm) (Rosenmund and Stevens, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Individual release events can be resolved at lower sucrose concentrations (+100 mOsm).
source: While high hypertonicity (+300 to +500 mOsm) causes the whole readily releasable pool to rapidly fuse, individual release events can be resolved at lower sucrose concentrations (+100 mOsm) (Rosenmund and Stevens, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Upon perfusion of +100 mOsm hypertonic sucrose, the spontaneous event frequency detected by iGluSnFR increased, while the amplitude of detected events remained the same.
source: Accordingly, upon perfusion of +100 mOsm hypertonic sucrose, the spontaneous event frequency detected by iGluSnFR increased, while the amplitude of detected events remained the same (Figure 3J, K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J, K.

claim: iGluSnFR detects quantal release for both evoked and spontaneous neurotransmission.
source: These results expand upon earlier work that validated iGluSnFR at single synapses (Farsi et al., 2021; Tagliatti et al., 2020), and demonstrate that iGluSnFR detects quantal release for both evoked and spontaneous neurotransmission.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and comparison to previous studies.

claim: The detection of different modes of release can be modulated by established parameters, such as Ca2+ and hypertonicity.
source: In these experiments, we also observed that the detection of these different modes of release can be modulated by established parameters, such as Ca2+ and hypertonicity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing modulation by Ca2+ and hypertonicity.

claim: iGluSnFR is a reliable and useful tool in measuring neurotransmitter release from single synapses.
source: These results show that iGluSnFR is a reliable and useful tool in measuring neurotransmitter release from single synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation experiments performed in the study.

claim: Photobleaching is a use-dependent process.
source: In contrast, fluorophores in the ground state (or nonfluorescent) cannot be photobleached, meaning that by its very nature, photobleaching is a use-dependent process (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of photobleaching, supported by a citation.

claim: In neurons, iGluSnFR is a very mobile probe, with similar recovery time constants between spine and shaft regions averaging 8.9 ± 7.0 and 9.9 ± 6.1 s, respectively.
source: In neurons, iGluSnFR is a very mobile probe, with similar recovery time constants between spine and shaft regions averaging 8.9 ± 7.0 and 9.9 ± 6.1 s, respectively (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: iGluSnFR exhibited an appreciable immobile fraction of 23% and 24% in spinous and shaft regions, respectively.
source: iGluSnFR also exhibited an appreciable immobile fraction of 23% and 24% in spinous and shaft regions, respectively (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Immobile fractions reflect a subpopulation of probes that cannot be replenished by nonbleached probes.
source: Immobile fractions reflect a subpopulation of probes that cannot be replenished by nonbleached probes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what immobile fractions represent in FRAP experiments.

claim: The existence of the immobile set of fluorophore molecules could be due to the geometry of the neuronal structure, for instance due to limitation of diffusion by surface proteins.
source: The existence of this immobile set of fluorophore molecules could be due to the geometry of the neuronal structure, for instance due to limitation of diffusion by surface proteins (Chen et al., 2021; Tardin et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the immobile fraction, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Another explanation for the immobile fraction could be that this is an intrinsic property of the probe, in which it interacts with proteins that tether it to the membrane surface.
source: Another explanation could be that this is an intrinsic property of the probe, in which it interacts with proteins that tether it to the membrane surface.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the immobile fraction.

claim: iGluSnFR is slightly more mobile in HEK cells (time constant of 5.6 ± 3.6 s) than in neurons.
source: We found that iGluSnFR is slightly more mobile in HEK cells (time constant of 5.6 ± 3.6 s) than in neurons (Figure 4H, I).

claim: iGluSnFR likely does not have an intrinsic property that leads it to tether to intracellular proteins.
source: This suggests that iGluSnFR likely does not have an intrinsic property that leads it to tether to intracellular proteins, and that limitations in diffusion may be partially due to the geometry and asymmetric composition of neuronal membranes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that iGluSnFR is more mobile in HEK cells than in neurons.

claim: Limitations in diffusion may be partially due to the geometry and asymmetric composition of neuronal membranes.
source: This suggests that iGluSnFR likely does not have an intrinsic property that leads it to tether to intracellular proteins, and that limitations in diffusion may be partially due to the geometry and asymmetric composition of neuronal membranes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that iGluSnFR is more mobile in HEK cells than in neurons.

claim: The immobile fraction was not significantly different in HEK cells compared to neurons.
source: We also observed that the immobile fraction was not significantly different in HEK cells compared to neurons (Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The increased mobility of iGluSnFR in HEK cells compared to neurons suggests that it is less likely that there is an intrinsic property of the probe that tethers it to a specific location on the plasma membrane surface but it rather arises from neuron-specific diffusion barriers.
source: Thus, the increased mobility of iGluSnFR in HEK cells compared to neurons suggests that it is less likely that there is an intrinsic property of the probe that tethers it to a specific location on the plasma membrane surface but it rather arises from neuron-specific diffusion barriers.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of iGluSnFR mobility in HEK cells versus neurons.

claim: After 30 s of photobleaching, the detection of spontaneous events decreased significantly but not completely.
source: After 30 s of photobleaching, the detection of spontaneous events decreased significantly but not completely.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from photobleaching experiments.

claim: At longer photobleaching periods of up to 20 min, spontaneous event frequency and amplitudes were decreased, although events remained detectable.
source: At longer photobleaching periods of up to 20 min, spontaneous event frequency and amplitudes were decreased, although events remained detectable (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B, C.

claim: Evoked release probability decreased significantly after 30 s of photobleaching.
source: Evoked release probability decreased significantly after 30 s.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from photobleaching experiments.

claim: Within 5–10 min of photobleaching, evoked release became largely undetectable.
source: And within 5–10 min, evoked release became largely undetectable (Figure 5D, E), demonstrating a significant difference in its rate of photobleaching compared to spontaneous neurotransmission (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D, E.

claim: There is a significant difference in the rate of photobleaching between evoked release and spontaneous neurotransmission.
source: And within 5–10 min, evoked release became largely undetectable (Figure 5D, E), demonstrating a significant difference in its rate of photobleaching compared to spontaneous neurotransmission (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D, E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Evoked release detection following photobleaching with stimulation was not different from photobleaching without stimulation.
source: We did not observe a difference in evoked release detection following photobleaching with stimulation versus without stimulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: One explanation for the lack of difference in evoked release detection with or without stimulation during photobleaching could be that spontaneous release during the photobleaching period is sufficient to occlude all evoked iGluSnFR responses.
source: One explanation could be that spontaneous release during the photobleaching period is sufficient to occlude all evoked iGluSnFR responses.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data.

claim: In the presence of 8 mM extracellular Ca2+, a higher degree of photobleaching of evoked responses was observed when electrical stimulation was applied during the bleaching period compared to nonstimulated neurons.
source: In agreement, we observed a higher degree of photobleaching of evoked responses when electrical stimulation was applied during the bleaching period in the presence of 8 mM extracellular Ca2+ compared to nonstimulated neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I), indicating that the level of photobleaching of evoked responses scales up with the amount of evoked glutamate release.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1I.

claim: The level of photobleaching of evoked responses scales up with the amount of evoked glutamate release.
source: In agreement, we observed a higher degree of photobleaching of evoked responses when electrical stimulation was applied during the bleaching period in the presence of 8 mM extracellular Ca2+ compared to nonstimulated neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I), indicating that the level of photobleaching of evoked responses scales up with the amount of evoked glutamate release.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that more photobleaching occurred with stimulation in high Ca2+.

claim: The results showing more photobleaching with stimulation in high Ca2+ could also be explained by reduced action potential firing due to reduced excitability in the presence of high calcium.
source: These results could also be explained by reduced action potential firing due to reduced excitability in the presence of high calcium (Segal, 2018).
evidence: This is an alternative speculative explanation for the observed data, supported by a citation.

claim: Spontaneous neurotransmission detected using iGluSnFR is more resilient to photobleaching than its evoked counterpart.
source: Our results so far indicate that spontaneous neurotransmission detected using iGluSnFR is more resilient to photobleaching than its evoked counterpart.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the photobleaching experiments.

claim: One interpretation is that iGluSnFR molecules activated by spontaneous release are in more mobile areas of the membrane and thus can be rapidly replaced by unbleached probes from other regions.
source: One interpretation is that iGluSnFR molecules activated by spontaneous release are in more mobile areas of the membrane and thus can be rapidly replaced by unbleached probes from other regions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the differential photobleaching results.

claim: Activating all iGluSnFR molecules during the photobleaching period should abolish future detection of spontaneous neurotransmission.
source: If this is the case, activating all iGluSnFR molecules during the photobleaching period should abolish future detection of spontaneous neurotransmission.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the interpretation that spontaneous release sites have more mobile iGluSnFR.

claim: The detection of spontaneous iGluSnFR events was significantly and nearly completely diminished after photobleaching during glutamate perfusion.
source: We found that the detection of spontaneous iGluSnFR events was significantly and nearly completely diminished after photobleaching during glutamate perfusion (Figure 5K).

claim: Activating all iGluSnFR probes at the plasma membrane during photobleaching eliminates event detection.
source: Thus, activating all iGluSnFR probes at the plasma membrane during photobleaching eliminates event detection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the glutamate perfusion during photobleaching experiment.

claim: The finding that activating all iGluSnFR probes during photobleaching eliminates event detection serves as a key negative control validating the specificity of the photobleaching approach toward bona fide glutamate release events.
source: Importantly, this finding serves as a key negative control validating the specificity of the photobleaching approach toward bona fide glutamate release events.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the significance of the glutamate perfusion experiment.

claim: Both spontaneous and evoked events were significantly bleached following the 10-min photobleaching period, although evoked events were relatively more susceptible to photobleaching.
source: Both spontaneous and evoked events were significantly bleached following the 10-min photobleaching period, although evoked events were relatively more susceptible to photobleaching confirming our previous findings.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the recovery experiments.

claim: Within an hour, spontaneous events were detectable at a frequency and amplitude that was similar to that prior to photobleaching.
source: Within an hour, spontaneous events were detectable at a frequency and amplitude that was similar to that prior to photobleaching (Figure 5H–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H–I.

claim: Evoked events remained undetectable an hour after photobleaching.
source: On the other hand, evoked events remained undetectable an hour after photobleaching.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the recovery experiments.

claim: After 8 hr, detection of evoked events resumed.
source: After 8 hr, detection of evoked events resumed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the recovery experiments.

claim: At 24 hr after photobleaching, evoked event values returned to their original pre-photobleaching values.
source: At 24 hr after photobleaching, evoked event values returned to their original pre-photobleaching values (Figure 5H, I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H, I.

claim: The recovery of spontaneous events occurred on the timescale of minutes, while the recovery of evoked events occurred on a longer timescale of hours.
source: By plotting the event rate over time, we found that the recovery of spontaneous events occurred on the timescale of minutes, while the recovery of evoked events occurred on a longer timescale of hours.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the recovery experiments.

claim: The slower recovery rate of evoked events suggests that iGluSnFR probes that respond to evoked release have less lateral mobility at the plasma membrane.
source: The slower recovery rate of evoked events suggests that iGluSnFR probes that respond to evoked release have less lateral mobility at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of slower recovery of evoked events.

claim: Photobleaching does not affect the frequency nor the amplitude of mEPSCs.

claim: The capacitance and membrane resistance of neurons are similar between control and photobleached neurons.
source: The capacitance and membrane resistance of neurons are indicative of membrane integrity and overall cell health, and these values were similar between control and photobleached neurons (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: There was no difference in the amplitude of evoked postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) between control and photobleached neurons.
source: Finally, we examined evoked excitatory neurotransmission (Figure 6D), and found no difference in the amplitude of evoked postsynaptic currents, or EPSCs (Figure 6E).

claim: There was no difference in the paired pulse ratio between control and photobleached neurons.

evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Photobleaching does not affect excitatory synaptic transmission as measured by electrophysiology, nor the resting properties of neurons.
source: These data show that photobleaching does not affect excitatory synaptic transmission as measured by electrophysiology, nor the resting properties of neurons.

claim: The decreases seen in iGluSnFR event detection reflect the effects of photobleaching on fluorescent probes, and not intrinsic changes in neurotransmission levels due to toxic effects of prolonged illumination.
